data.title: 【財經皓角專訪】賴清德總統談台灣經濟
data.transcript_raw: Hello investors, welcome to the  Financial Horn channel. Today, we  invite our channel's first guest to the  studio: President Lai, it's an honor to  have you. >> Hello, Ting-Hao, and hello to all our  viewers. President, in the last two  days, I reviewed some of your previous  financial interviews. You've been on  Unique Business News, MacroMicro, and  President Hsieh’s program. I took a  look back. I realized those were all  major productions with large teams and  TV stations. How are we so fortunate to  have you here to share your industrial  policies? What made you willing to come  on our show? >> Ting-Hao, I’ll be honest, it is my  honor to be on your show. >> Oh, I wouldn't say that. You are a  young, sharp talent, and your grasp of  macroeconomics is so skilled and yet  very relatable. >> Hmm. >> And you are very dedicated, from 8:30  to 9:00 every day, before the stock  market opens, >> you share your insights on the entire  industrial economy and the financial  landscape. I have always considered you  a "God of Wealth." >> Oh, really? >> Yes, you are effectively sharing your  financial knowledge with all your  listeners and viewers. >> I think it’s truly fantastic. That is  perhaps the highest compliment I have  ever heard for our channel. Netizens  give us decent reviews too, but usually  not quite like what you’ve described.  Alright, today we will explore things  across six major aspects. In economics,  it is often called the science of " trade-offs" because resources are  limited. Our six aspects mainly explore  the order of priority when various  resources and policy goals come into  conflict. Please feel free to speak  your mind. If the six aspects happen to  echo the previous topics, feel free to  bring them up directly. Since the  script is not great, let’s just have  a conversation. People might think we  scripted this, which wouldn't be good  for you, so just say whatever comes to  mind naturally. Great, the first major  topic is about our AI policy. We have  an AI initiative, an AI cabinet, and an  "AI President." Since a series of AI  policies began, they have been keeping  pace with the global trend of AI-driven  economic growth. There is a perspective  now that the industrial upgrades of the  1980s were at the forefront, benefiting  80%of the people, whereas the 2026 AI  explosion is cutting-edge but only  benefits 10%of the ICT industry. >> We also know that AI policy is heavily  absorbing resources, whether it’s  water, electricity, or talent, and even  financial lending is being rapidly  steered toward it. This has led to such  a massive tilt of resources toward AI  that many polls in the U.S. now show  that people opposing AI data centers  outnumber those who support them. Your  policy direction to promote AI is  correct, but how do we know whether we  should continue expanding AI or pivot  back to regulating it? How do we  balance the two? >> Yes, thank you for that question. I  realized that the world has entered the  era of artificial intelligence, so  early in my term, I actively initiated  legislation called the Artificial  Intelligence Basic Act. This basic law  consists of seven principles. When  promoting AI development, the first is  to ensure social sustainability, and  the second is that human autonomy must  not ultimately be controlled by AI. Mm. >> The third is that we must respect  privacy, as data is the most important  part of AI, so we must be mindful of  data acquisition and usage. The fourth  is security; security is extremely  important. The fifth is that it must be  open, transparent, and explainable, and  the sixth is that we must ensure  fairness and avoid discrimination. >> That covers the sixth and seventh,  which is accountability. So, as you can  see, my answer is that the government  must act as a responsible promoter.  These seven principles represent the  way we exercise that responsibility.  Secondly, the government must, of  course, promote AI development, but we  must do so steadily within the  framework of these seven principles. As  you just mentioned, we proposed the "AI  Era Ten Major Infrastructure Projects,"  which includes four foundations: the  first is human talent cultivation,  aiming to train at least 500,000 AI  application professionals by 2040. The  second is to build computing power and  AI sovereign centers; the third is a  stable power supply; and the fourth is  to ensure balanced development across  Taiwan. Of course, the AI Era Ten Major  Infrastructure Projects also focus on  three key core technologies: silicon  photonics, quantum computing, and  robotics. Ultimately, we hope to  achieve three goals. The first is to  assist at least one million small and  medium-sized enterprises to adopt  artificial intelligence and  successfully undergo digital  transformation by 2040. The second goal  is to build an ecosystem for innovation  and entrepreneurship. And by 2040, we  aim to reach one trillion NT dollars in  software industry output. As for the  third goal, we hope that in the Taiwan  of the future, all aspects of daily  life—food, clothing, housing,  transportation, education,  entertainment, agriculture, industry,  and commerce—can utilize AI, making  Taiwan an AI-driven living sphere. In  this living sphere, we hope to rank  among the top five countries in the  world in terms of AI application and  development. Hmm. >> Of course, what you just mentioned is a  valid concern—that is, will it suck  up all the resources, making it harder  for other industries to develop?  However, the public may not have  noticed the government's efforts over  the past decade. Whether it's water,  electricity, land, or talent, we have  basically been pursuing balanced  development. For example, regarding  water, we have created the "Pearl  String" project for the western region. >> We have connected all the reservoirs,  ponds, and dams in the west. Using  interconnected pipelines, they are  linked together like a string of pearls . Like a pearl necklace. And so, water  can flow from the north to the south.  As for electricity, there is no need to  worry; we have already taken stock,  accounting for the electricity demand  of our future economic growth. We have  calculated the power requirements,  including the energy needs for the  development of the AI industry. >> Stable power supply is guaranteed  through 2035. What is my goal, then? It  is to see the semiconductor industry  thrive while other industries also grow ; that is the government's objective.  That seems quite clear, providing both  development and regulation. The  President's push for AI, or rather the  promotion of AI policy, is also a major  policy direction. At this point, I am  also curious about something, because  you mentioned a very important point:  that having "every industry use AI" is  more important than simply pushing AI  trends. In the process of promoting AI  across all industries, some may wonder —if you want to increase productivity  and reduce repetitive tasks, and since  the government itself is a huge entity —shouldn't the government be the one  to set the example first? Perhaps you  could streamline some administrative  procedures yourself, or even control  government spending. Otherwise, with  the advent of AI, it seems like there  are more AI national teams and AI  policy committees, and AI spending has  increased, yet it doesn't seem to have  helped us cut costs very much. As a  government, shouldn't we be setting an  example? >> To put it simply, of the three goals I  just mentioned, the most important  overarching national goal is a Smart  Nation. >> A Smart Nation naturally includes what  we mentioned: smart production, >> smart manufacturing, as well as smart  tourism and smart living. But a key  part of that, and the question you're  asking right now, is a Smart Government . >> Mm. >> Currently, we have an Economic Security  Council at the Presidential Office  where we are discussing what a Smart  Government should look like. Just last  week, the Ministry of Economic Affairs,  the Ministry of Digital Affairs, and  the Financial Supervisory Commission  reported on how to use AI to assist  them, making their work more efficient  and improving services; we are indeed  moving in that direction. Okay, hearing  you say that, I suppose I can consider  you a tech optimist. Because you have  to understand that many in the  financial sector are bullish on AI, but  not necessarily on all AI assets, due  to potential issues with  off-balance-sheet financing, financing  cycles, and the capitalization of GPU  chips. Many people believe that  technology will continue to  revolutionize, but there may be  financial risks behind it. If the  government pours so much effort into a  single AI policy, what if financial  problems arise overseas and affect  orders for Taiwan? Wouldn't that be  another type of risk? Will that be  considered in your policy? >> Of course. It is true that we are  constantly monitoring how the  development of AI has created such  strong demand for servers and  semiconductors, which is why Taiwan's  economy is doing well. The second point  is, what if? Because of some issues,  like the duplicate investments you just  mentioned or other reasons, what if  this demand drops? We are indeed  preparing various contingency measures. >> Okay. >> We are not entirely, >> we don't see it as absolutely  optimistic or a guaranteed outcome, but  we are certainly making preparations;  however, personally, as you know, I am  not trained in finance, >> so I am looking at this from >> the user's perspective. >> From the perspective of a user or from  the perspective of historical  development. >> Mm. >> Through the invention of the steam  engine, which drove the Industrial  Revolution and gave Europe 200 years of  civilization and prosperity. >> That was the beginning of the  Industrial Revolution. >> And now we have just entered the age of  artificial intelligence; it’s only  just begun. >> OK, this is just the beginning. >> It is only just the beginning, so I’m  saying, as president, what is my  responsibility? It is to ensure that as  the world enters the era of artificial  intelligence, Taiwan must continue to  occupy an advantageous position. >> Mm. >> To ensure the next 30 years, perhaps 50  years, or even longer. >> Of competitive advantage, that is  currently >> the focus of all my efforts. >> You are personally optimistic about AI,  so do you personally >> Basically, I am optimistic. Do you use  any AI, for example, ChatGPT or... >> Yes, before I came on your show, I did  a little bit of Googling. >> I see, so you probably don’t use  DeepSeek. >> No, no, okay. >> The government prohibits public  agencies from using DeepSeek. OK, good,  good, then no problem with the first  question. Now for the second part, we  want to talk about the potential side  effects of AI within the policy  framework, specifically regarding the  issue of wealth distribution from AI.  We keep talking about the K-shaped  economy, the K-shaped economy.  Currently, the president has proposed  salary increases, tax cuts, and  reducing the government burden; the  policy direction is very clear. But  some people think that perhaps a  balance could be struck between primary  and secondary distribution. What does  that mean? The government currently  provides many benefits, such as tax  relief, social welfare, and policies  related to raising wages for domestic  workers and hiring foreign labor.  Essentially, it seems that businesses  make money first, the government  collects taxes, and then the government  uses those taxes for subsidies, which  seems to be part of secondary  distribution. Some people might place  greater importance on primary  distribution. For example, the recent  controversies involving companies like  Kuai Kuai or Micron actually illustrate  that many workers hope that since  businesses are making huge profits and  have already received tax breaks and AI  subsidies, shouldn't they distribute a  certain percentage of that as  compensation to employees within the  same year? Do you think that primary  distribution is a direction the  government needs to focus more on now?  For instance, through support for labor  unions, or in the process of companies  receiving subsidies, should we also  impose relative requirements that they  must pay more money to their employees?  What is your view? >> Well, thank you. I believe that  management and labor are like water  helping fish and fish helping water.  Regarding the current demands from the  employees of the Meiguang company, I  hope we can take more time. And show  greater sincerity to sit down and talk.  Then come up with a mutually acceptable  plan to achieve a win-win for both  labor and management. This would be  good for the company, good for the  workers, and actually good for Taiwan's  overall labor environment. Secondly,  you mentioned at the beginning whether  developing the AI industry will lead to  a K-shaped economy. This is a concern  of mine as President, and it is also  addressed in the first of the seven  principles of our AI Basic Law, which  is sustainable development. That is to  say, when developing artificial  intelligence, we must not widen the  wealth gap, >> leading to a K-shaped economy; that is  not what we want. What we want is  sustainable social development. So, how  will I do it? First, I will prevent the  polarization of Taiwan's industries.  That is, avoiding a situation where  only tech industries or only the  semiconductor industry exist. We must  avoid this polarization, so how do I do  that? First, besides assisting the  continued development of the tech  industry, we have proposed the Act for  the Upgrading and Transformation of  Small and Medium Enterprises, using a  set of laws. In my speech on May 20th  this year marking my second anniversary , I also proposed a 100 billion fund. >> Mm. >> To assist small and medium enterprises  in upgrading and transforming. The  third point, which I think is even more  important, is for large enterprises to  lead small ones. >> Looking back at Taiwan's industrial  history, agriculture supported  industrial development, and later, as  industry developed, it turned back to  drive agricultural development, leading  to agricultural modernization. >> Starting over 30 years ago, industry  supported the technology sector. Now  that the tech industry has developed  successfully, it should return the  favor by driving industrial development , especially for traditional industries  and SMEs. How do we do that? Small and  medium enterprises and traditional  industries need to integrate into the  tech industry's supply chain. >> So, we are now grateful to TSMC for  their willingness to help, and  additionally, TSMC and ASE have  established a packaging and testing  supply chain in Kaohsiung's Nanzih. In  this supply chain, if an enterprise  wants to enter this packaging and  testing ecosystem, you can do it  on-site. >> You can test right there. >> Mm. And once successful, you can enter  the supply chain. We hope that the  large can lead the small to avoid a  situation where the big get bigger and  the small get smaller. If this "large  leading small" approach succeeds, I  believe it will be a blessing for  Taiwan's industrial development.  Meaning, big companies make money. And  small companies can also make money. >> Only then can employees share in the  profits. ... >> so that employees can actually receive  it, especially for the 1.71 million  SMEs with as many as 9 million workers.  The second point is that we must  continue, my second approach is to  promote infrastructure construction. >> I have launched an infrastructure  development plan, what does this  include? It includes transportation,  water... >> Social housing. >> Mm. >> Healthcare and so on, as well as the  tourism industry. Including green  energy, why do we do this? Because by  having these other industries  continuously pushed forward, there will  be jobs for the population. >> This is to maintain the middle class.  Mm. >> The middle class is the stabilizing  force of society. >> OK. >> The third point is to avoid the  continued widening of the wealth gap,  which is what you just mentioned. We  are expanding social investment. >> From President Tsai's term to my own,  over these 10 years, we have  continuously promoted four directions:  raising wages, cutting taxes,  increasing benefits, and reducing  burdens. >> Regarding wage increases, for the past  11 consecutive years, we have adjusted  the minimum wage. When President Ma  handed over to President Tsai, it was  20,008 NTD. And now, it has already  reached 30,900 NTD. Additionally, over  these 10 years, we have raised salaries  for military, public, and educational  personnel five times. Roughly speaking,  if you include professional allowances  and supervisory additions, it's about  20%. >> Also, I am particularly concerned about  public safety, so I gave police  detectives a raise. We have increased  their duty allowances and danger pay.  And for the military, I have also  increased their grade-based allowances.  Because soldiers are there to protect  the country. Police officers are there  to maintain social order. >> So we keep raising wages, and we also  cut taxes. I think you know  macroeconomics better than me, as a  percentage of GDP, we are only at about  13-something percent. >> That is, Taiwan's tax... >> burden rate is not that high. >> The tax burden rate is not that high,  it's just over 13 percent. The U.S. is  over 19%, Japan is 20%, other G7  countries are around 30%to 35%, and  many European countries are around 35% to 45%. So Taiwan keeps cutting taxes.  For individuals, as you just said,  about 45%of the public doesn't need to  pay income tax. >> The top 1%pay 45%of total income taxes;  this means we take from the surplus to  support those in need. That's how we  approach raising wages and cutting  taxes. Regarding increasing benefits  and reducing burdens, starting from  President Tsai, we've had the "0 to 6  years old, raised by the state" policy. >> It's 5,000 NTD for the first child,  6,000 for the second, and 7,000 for the  third, every month. And in my mission,  I’ve added tuition-free high school  and vocational school, whether public  or private. >> Mm. >> For private colleges and universities,  we provide tuition subsidies. 35,000  per year, with an extra 20,000 for  low-income and 10,000 for  middle-low-income households. Also,  long-term care has reached 3.0; there  are now over 15,000 long-term care  centers across Taiwan, with over  100,000 caregivers looking after  seniors and the disabled. This year,  we’ve proposed a program for those  aged zero to eighteen. This growth  subsidy means every child between zero  and eighteen can receive 5,000 NT  dollars per month. I believe we are the  first country in the world to do this.  I believe this will ensure that, for  our future children, no matter what  family they are born into, as long as  they want to study, >> they will have government support to go  to school, changing their lives through  education. When individuals thrive, the  nation and society naturally thrive as  well. That is the ultimate goal of all  our work. You mentioned the middle  class earlier. Of course, some  middle-class citizens might have  different views, thinking that while  the social welfare is good, we’ve  been handing out cash to everyone  recently. >> Many in the middle class might wonder  why these cash handouts aren’t based  on the amount of taxes paid. Some might  think, "I have to raise children, pay  taxes, pay off car loans, and pay my  mortgage.""AI giants get so many tax  subsidies, and low-income households  get corresponding social welfare, yet  I’m the one paying most of the heavy  taxes, and now you’re using my money  for universal cash handouts." Could the  middle class actually be the ones  suffering under these welfare policies  in a K-shaped economy? How do you view  this issue? >> It’s like this: as we discussed  earlier, 50%of the income tax is paid  by the top 1%of earners. >> Mm. >> They pay it. >> Mm. If we were to distribute AI  dividends proportionally based on taxes  paid, the corporations would end up  getting it. >> Right, they’d get it back. Secondly,  we have to recognize that every single  person contributes to the economy. >> It shouldn’t be judged solely by  taxes paid. Take a taxi driver, for  example. >> They also contribute a lot to Taiwan. >> Or a cleaning staff member. They allow  the entire company or hospital to  operate smoothly, which is a  significant contribution. Therefore,  when we distribute these AI dividends,  we should look at it from an individual  perspective, rather than using income  or tax contributions as the sole  criteria. We should look at the big  picture. Exactly. And especially for  the middle class you just mentioned, we  have other social welfare systems to  support them. >> For example, the "Zero to Six, the  State Raises Them" initiative we just  mentioned. >> Or the growth subsidies for those aged  zero to eighteen, tuition-free public  and private high schools, subsidies for  private college tuition, and even  long-term care 2.0. These are actually  helpful for "sandwich" families. Mm. >> Families who are supporting both their  parents and their own children—these  sandwich families—are greatly helped  by this. Mm. When we talk about a  K-shaped economy, we sometimes touch  upon generational conflicts. It feels  like those at the bottom of the  K-shaped economy, the youth, are having  a harder time. The government has  pushed many policies, especially in  housing, like rental subsidies, youth  housing loans, and so on. However, the  values of many young people today seem  to be shifting. There's a popular term  going around: "the three nos"—no  mortgage, no car loan, and no children.  One perspective is that the external  environment is just too harsh, making  it impossible for them to even think  about settling down or pursuing a  career, so they might just choose to " lie flat." It's not just a question of  marriage; they might not even consider  dating. Every day they might just take  it easy, maybe go for a picnic, and try  to relax. But for an individual, I  don't see a problem with that; young  people have their own thoughts and  ideas. However, if many young people  feel this way, rising to your level— the presidential level—do you think  this is a problem? What would you like  to say to these young people? Yes, this  is indeed a problem. If the social  atmosphere reaches this point, it is  certainly something that is very... >> very worthy of social attention, yes.  The experience I want to share with  these young people is that while your  life is your own, life isn't just  divided into segments; it’s a journey  from birth to death that can last  decades or even longer. So, when you  view things from the perspective of  being young, you will naturally have  certain thoughts, but if you take a  longer view, perhaps your outlook will  be different. >> I also hope that everyone can have a  wonderful, fulfilling life that meets  their own needs. >> But as president, my hope is to create  better conditions. >> Mm. Because if I encourage raising  children, then I should build a better  environment for raising them, so young  people are willing to do so without  worries. >> That is why I just mentioned the 0-to- 18 growth fund; it is only one part of  it. We recently released our National  Population Strategy, focusing on family  support. Mm. >> Besides the 0-to-18 growth fund, we are  specifically looking at three stages:  childbirth, child-rearing, and  education. We have also proposed  subsidies for childbirth. And for  affordable childcare, we also provide  educational subsidies. And housing. >> Mm. >> And a friendly workplace, meaning we
